   - `publication_year`: 4-digit year printed on the paper/report itself (e.g. `"2024"`), or `"not reported"` if undated. Give exact page/header in `where_found`.

   - `study_design`: Study design as the authors describe it and as operationalized in the methods section (be specific about quantitative/qualitative/quasi-experimental/experimental/review structure).
   - `effect_estimate`: Headline result of the study regarding how the legal, administrative, regulatory, institutional, tenure, tariff/subsidy, or participation factor relates to water/sanitation access/outcomes, with exact printed numbers (point estimates, units, 95% CIs, p-values, sample N) if quantitative, or concise factual headline finding if qualitative (noting `"Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported"` when purely qualitative), in your own words from the paper alone.
   - `risk_of_bias_tool`: Pick the single design-matched tool per `RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1:
     * `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"` (individually randomized trial)
     * `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"` (cluster-randomized trial — check unit of randomization carefully!)
     * `"ROBINS-I"` (non-randomized intervention / quasi-experimental study with a genuine comparator: DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, policy panel FE)
     * `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"` (quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without quasi-experimental intervention comparator)
     * `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"` (observational longitudinal cohort study without intervention framing)
     * `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"` (primary qualitative study: interviews, focus groups, ethnography, qualitative case study)
     * `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"` (genuine mixed-methods study combining both qualitative and quantitative primary components)
     * `"AMSTAR 2"` (systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with systematic search/screening; NEVER use for non-systematic narrative literature reviews)
     * `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"` (legal-empirical, doctrinal-empirical, jurimetric, or institutional-historical study that fits none of the six conventional designs above)
     * `"NONE"` (fits none of the listed tools, e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model, or non-systematic narrative review/essay without primary empirical data or systematic search — explain why in `comment`)

     * All other designs (cross-sectional/JBI, cohort, qualitative/CASP, mixed-methods/MMAT, systematic review/AMSTAR 2, Legal Framework, NONE, or Serious/Critical ROBINS-I) CANNOT exceed `"2"`! (`"2"` = mechanism directly observed empirically; `"1"` = documented statistical/descriptive association; `"0"` = inferred only by authors).

country.comment: The realist review focuses exclusively on drinking water policy in Australia across national, state/territory, and local levels (non-Australian literature was excluded per Section 2.7).
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 2, Section 1; PDF pp. 3–4, Section 2.7

effect_estimate.comment: Purely qualitative realist synthesis of secondary literature and policy documents; any numeric figures cited in the results (e.g., 408 remote/regional communities lacking safe drinking water, >500 remote communities with minimal water quality monitoring) are descriptive context drawn from included reports rather than a primary quantitative effect estimate.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Across 38 included sources, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander involvement in Australian drinking water policy is fragmented, inconsistent, and not legally mandated across national, state/territory, and local levels. National Australian Drinking Water Guidelines lack regulatory enforcement and the human right to safe drinking water is not enshrined in enforceable national, state, or local legislation, reinforcing urban versus rural/remote disparities (citing secondary findings that 408 remote and regional communities—40% Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander—lack safe drinking water and over 500 remote communities have minimal water quality monitoring). Overcoming entrenched drinking water inequities requires embedding Indigenous governance, self-determination, cultural knowledges, and long-term funding for transparent shared decision-making across macro, meso, and micro policy levels.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 8–10, Sections 3.1–3.9 and Figure 2; PDF pp. 10–11, Section 4

mechanism_certainty.comment: As a secondary realist review appraised with AMSTAR 2, the study is subject to a design ceiling of at most 2. Rated 1 because it synthesizes secondary policy documents, commentaries, and reviews documenting descriptive institutional gaps (fragmented multi-level governance, non-enforceable national guidelines, and unmandated Indigenous participation) alongside remote drinking water disparities, while explicitly noting in Section 5 that the authors could not locate local government reports or case studies comprehensively linking mechanisms and outcomes in drinking water policy.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 8–10, Sections 3.3–3.8; PDF p. 11, Section 5; PDF pp. 15–18, Appendix A

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines Indigenous participation/co-design and shared decision-making in water policy (participation), cultural tailoring and integration of Indigenous knowledge systems versus mainstream one-size-fits-all policy (accommodation), fragmented and misaligned responsibilities and complex bureaucratic navigation across national, state/territory, and local governments (institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination, BURDEN), and the absence of statutory human-rights obligations or regulatory enforcement of national drinking water standards (ENFORCEMENT).
